## Quick Summary

Every piece of hardware that is not a disk — a serial port, a USB gadget, a virtual
console, a network tap — reaches userland through the same two-part contract. The
driver owns a `struct cdevsw`, a table of function pointers named `d_open`,
`d_read`, `d_write`, `d_ioctl`, `d_poll`, and `d_kqfilter`. When a process calls
[`open(2)`](../../lib/libsys/open.2) on a `/dev` [node](../netgraph/README.md#glossary), the kernel walks from the vnode back to that table and
calls the right pointer. The driver never touches the path name, the permissions,
the file descriptor, or the copy between user and kernel buffers; those are handled
by the layers below it. This chapter is the second half of driver authorship: the
Device Driver Framework chapter explains how a driver *attaches* to hardware; this
one explains how it *exposes* that hardware as something a process can read from.

The `/dev` directory is not a real directory on a real disk. It is a filesystem
called devfs that the kernel populates on demand: each `make_dev()` call registers a
`cdev` in an in-kernel list, and devfs turns that list into vnodes that `lookup(9)`
can find. Because the entries are generated, not stored, the kernel can hand a
different `/dev` to every jail by running a [ruleset](../netpfil/pf/README.md#glossary) over the same list. A device
that exists in the base system can be hidden, renamed, or re-owned in a jail without
touching the driver at all.

The terminal is the most-used character device, and it is where a byte stream
becomes a line. The TTY core in `sys/kern/tty.c` owns the queues; the line
discipline in `sys/kern/tty_ttydisc.c` decides what a byte *means*. In canonical
mode it accumulates input until a newline, echoes what you type, and turns the
special characters (Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Z, Ctrl-U) into signals aimed at the foreground
process group. Pseudo-terminals in `sys/kern/tty_pts.c` are two `tty` structures
wired back to back, which is what lets `sshd`, `xterm`, and [`script(1)`](../../usr.bin/script/script.1) present a
shell with a terminal behind it even though no physical serial line exists.

## Architecture

The character-device abstraction lives in three files. `sys/kern/kern_conf.c`
implements `make_dev()` and `destroy_dev()` and keeps the single in-kernel list of
live devices, `cdevp_list`, guarded by the `devmtx` mutex. `sys/sys/conf.h` defines
`struct cdev`, `struct cdevsw`, and the `d_*` typedefs. `sys/fs/devfs/` is the
filesystem that turns those `cdev`s into vnodes: `devfs_devs.c` owns the list and
the `devfs_create()`/`devfs_destroy()` bookkeeping, `devfs_vnops.c` implements the
vnode operations that dispatch to the `d_*` methods, and `devfs_rule.c` implements
the per-jail ruleset engine.

The data path for a read is short and worth tracing once. Userland calls [`read(2)`](../../lib/libsys/read.2)
on a file descriptor that points at a devfs vnode. The VFS layer calls the vnode's
`vop_foffread` entry, which for devfs is `devfs_read_f()` in `devfs_vnops.c`. That
function calls `devfs_fp_check()` to resolve the file back to its `cdev` and
`cdevsw`, then invokes `devsw->d_read(dev, uio, ioflag, cred, td)`. The driver's
`d_read` copies bytes into the `struct uio` that the system call already built;
the actual user/kernel copy is done by `uiomove()` in `sys/kern/subr_uio.c`, the
same engine behind every `d_read`/`d_write` in the kernel. Note the layering: the
driver sees a `uio`, not a user pointer, so it never has to call `copyin`/`copyout`
itself.

The TTY layer sits on top of the same machinery. A terminal driver (the serial
port `uart`, the virtual console, the null-modem `nmdm`) does not implement
`d_read`/`d_write` itself; it implements a `struct ttydevsw` — the `tsw_*` table in
`sys/sys/ttydevsw.h` — and registers it with `tty_alloc()`. The TTY core's
`cdevsw` (`ttydevsw` in `sys/kern/tty.c`) handles the generic `d_open`/`d_read`/
`d_write`/`d_ioctl`/`d_poll` and calls the driver's `tsw_*` callbacks only for the
hardware-specific parts: setting baud rate (`tsw_param`), asserting modem lines
(`tsw_modem`), and waking the other side of a link (`tsw_inwakeup`/`tsw_outwakeup`).
The line discipline in `tty_ttydisc.c` is the part that interprets bytes; it is
pluggable, which is why the same `tty` can run the standard `termios` discipline or
a raw one.

One note on scope: block devices no longer go through this path. The legacy
`d_strategy`/`physio` mechanism is gone and disks are handled by [GEOM](../vm/README_bcache.md#glossary) and g_vfs, so
`cdev` is effectively the only device abstraction a driver uses to expose anything
to userland. We say that once and move on.
## Key Data Structures

`struct cdev` is the device instance. It is defined in `sys/sys/conf.h` and is
embedded, by value, as the first field of `struct cdev_priv`:

```c
/* sys/sys/conf.h */
struct cdev {
	void		*si_spare0;
	u_int		si_flags;
#define	SI_ETERNAL	0x0001	/* never destroyed */
#define	SI_ALIAS	0x0002	/* carrier of alias name */
#define	SI_NAMED	0x0004	/* make_dev{_alias} has been called */
	...
	struct ucred	*si_cred;	/* cached clone-time credential */
	int		si_drv0;
	int		si_refcount;
	LIST_ENTRY(cdev)	si_list;
	LIST_ENTRY(cdev)	si_clone;
	LIST_HEAD(, cdev)	si_children;
	LIST_ENTRY(cdev)	si_siblings;
	struct cdev *si_parent;
	struct mount	*si_mountpt;
	void		*si_drv1, *si_drv2;
	struct cdevsw	*si_devsw;
	int		si_iosize_max;	/* maximum I/O size (for physio &al) */
	u_long		si_usecount;
	u_long		si_threadcount;
	char		si_name[SPECNAMELEN + 1];
};
```

The two fields a driver cares about most are `si_drv1` (a single `void *` the
driver uses to point at its per-device [softc](README_driver.md#glossary) — this is how `evdev_open` below
recovers its `evdev_dev`) and `si_devsw` (the pointer to the method table). The
`si_refcount`/`si_usecount` pair is the reason device destruction is deferred: a
`cdev` cannot be freed while any [thread](README_process.md#glossary) holds it open, so `destroy_dev()` only
marks it and frees it later, once the counts drain.

`struct cdevsw` is the method table. It is a static, per-driver object; the
`d_version` field must be `D_VERSION` so the kernel can reject a table built against
a different kernel. A real initializer, from `sys/dev/evdev/cdev.c`:

```c
/* sys/dev/evdev/cdev.c */
static struct cdevsw evdev_cdevsw = {
	.d_version = D_VERSION,
	.d_open = evdev_open,
	.d_read = evdev_read,
	.d_write = evdev_write,
	.d_ioctl = evdev_ioctl,
	.d_poll = evdev_poll,
	.d_kqfilter = evdev_kqfilter,
	.d_name = "evdev",
};
```

The full type, from `sys/sys/conf.h`, lists the methods in order:

```c
/* sys/sys/conf.h (method table) */
struct cdevsw {
	int		d_version;	/* must be set to D_VERSION */
	u_int		d_flags;	/* must be set to 0 */
	const char	*d_name;
	d_open_t	*d_open;
	d_fdopen_t	*d_fdopen;
	d_close_t	*d_close;
	d_read_t	*d_read;
	d_write_t	*d_write;
	d_ioctl_t	*d_ioctl;
	d_poll_t	*d_poll;
	d_kqfilter_t	*d_kqfilter;
	d_mmap_t	*d_mmap;
	d_strategy_t	*d_strategy;
	/* ... */
};
```

`d_fdopen` is the variant of `d_open` that also receives the `struct file *`, used
when a driver needs to [attach](README_driver.md#glossary) per-file private data (see `cdev_privdata` below).
`d_kqfilter` returns a `struct filterops *` for [`kqueue(2)`](../../lib/libsys/kqueue.2); `d_poll` is the
[`poll(2)`](../../lib/libsys/poll.2)/[`select(2)`](../../lib/libsys/select.2) path.

`struct cdev_priv` is the wrapper devfs actually allocates. It is defined in
`sys/fs/devfs/devfs_int.h`, a private header shared only by `kern_conf.c` and
`fs/devfs`. The reason it exists is to keep the public `struct cdev` clean: the
inode number (the filesystem-level identifier that [stat(2)](../../lib/libsys/stat.2) reports as st_ino), the
dirent (directory-entry) array, and the per-open private-data list are devfs
concerns, not driver concerns, so they live in the wrapper.

```c
/* sys/fs/devfs/devfs_int.h */
struct cdev_priv {
	struct cdev		cdp_c;
	TAILQ_ENTRY(cdev_priv)	cdp_list;

	u_int			cdp_inode;

	u_int			cdp_flags;
#define CDP_ACTIVE		(1 << 0)
#define CDP_SCHED_DTR		(1 << 1)
#define	CDP_UNREF_DTR		(1 << 2)
#define CDP_ON_ACTIVE_LIST	(1 << 3)

	u_int			cdp_inuse;
	u_int			cdp_maxdirent;
	struct devfs_dirent	**cdp_dirents;
	struct devfs_dirent	*cdp_dirent0;

	TAILQ_ENTRY(cdev_priv)	cdp_dtr_list;
	void			(*cdp_dtr_cb)(void *);
	void			*cdp_dtr_cb_arg;

	LIST_HEAD(, cdev_privdata) cdp_fdpriv;
	u_int			cdp_fdpriv_dtrc;

	struct mtx		cdp_threadlock;
};

#define	cdev2priv(c)	__containerof(c, struct cdev_priv, cdp_c)
```

`cdp_inode` is the `dev_t` — the number [`stat(2)`](../../lib/libsys/stat.2) reports and [`devname(3)`](../../lib/libc/gen/devname.3) looks
back up. `cdp_dirents` is the array of devfs directory entries this device
materializes (a clone device with several names has several dirents). `cdp_fdpriv`
holds the per-file private data; `devfs_get_cdevpriv()`/`devfs_set_cdevpriv()` are
the API a driver uses to stash a pointer there so it survives across [`read(2)`](../../lib/libsys/read.2) and
[`ioctl(2)`](../../lib/libsys/ioctl.2) calls on the same descriptor.

The per-jail visibility is driven by `struct devfs_rule`, defined in
`sys/fs/devfs/devfs.h`. A rule is a pure value (no pointers) so it can be shared
verbatim between kernel and userland — [`devfs(8)`](../../sbin/devfs/devfs.8) and `devfs(5)` build rulesets
from these. The `dr_icond`/`dr_iacts` bitfields select which conditions and actions
are active:

```c
/* sys/fs/devfs/devfs.h */
struct devfs_rule {
	uint32_t dr_magic;			/* Magic number. */
	devfs_rid dr_id;			/* Identifier. */
	int	dr_icond;
#define	DRC_DSWFLAGS	0x001
#define	DRC_PATHPTRN	0x002
	int	dr_dswflags;			/* cdevsw flags to match. */
	char	dr_pathptrn[DEVFS_MAXPTRNLEN];	/* Pattern to match path. */
	int	dr_iacts;
#define	DRA_BACTS		0x001
#define	DRA_UID		0x002
#define	DRA_GID		0x004
#define	DRA_MODE		0x008
#define	DRA_INCSET		0x010
	int	dr_bacts;			/* Boolean (on/off) action. */
#define	DRB_HIDE	0x001			/* Hide entry (DE_WHITEOUT). */
#define	DRB_UNHIDE	0x002			/* Unhide entry. */
	uid_t	dr_uid;
	gid_t	dr_gid;
	mode_t	dr_mode;
	devfs_rsnum dr_incset;			/* Included ruleset. */
};
```

`DRB_HIDE` is the workhorse for jails: a rule that matches a path pattern and sets
`dr_bacts = DRB_HIDE` makes that node a whiteout (`DE_WHITEOUT`), so the path
resolves to "not found" inside the jail but still exists in the base system.
On the TTY side, `struct tty` (in `sys/sys/tty.h`) is the per-terminal [state](../netpfil/pf/README.md#glossary). The
first fields, read directly from the header, are:

```c
/* sys/sys/tty.h */
struct tty {
	struct mtx	*t_mtx;		/* TTY lock. */
	struct mtx	t_mtxobj;	/* Per-TTY lock (when not borrowing). */
	TAILQ_ENTRY(tty) t_list;	/* (l) TTY list entry. */
	int		t_drainwait;	/* (t) TIOCDRAIN timeout seconds. */
	unsigned int	t_flags;	/* (t) Terminal option flags. */
	...
	unsigned int	t_revokecnt;	/* (t) revoke() count. */

	/* Buffering mechanisms. */
	struct ttyinq	t_inq;		/* (t) Input queue. */
	size_t		t_inlow;	/* (t) Input low watermark. */
	struct ttyoutq	t_outq;		/* (t) Output queue. */
	size_t		t_outlow;	/* (t) Output low watermark. */
	...
};
```

Beyond the truncation point, the fields the line discipline and job control rely on
are `t_termios` (the `struct termios` holding the `c_iflag`/`c_lflag`/`c_cc`
settings), `t_pgrp` (the foreground process group, the target of terminal-generated
signals), `t_session` (the owning session), `t_devsw` (the `struct ttydevsw *`), and
`t_devswsoftc` (the driver's softc, reachable through the `tty_softc(tp)` macro).
The `(t)` and `(l)` annotations in the header are a locking map: `(t)` means the
field is protected by `t_mtx`, `(l)` by the global `tty_list_sx`.

The two queues are block lists, not ring buffers. `struct ttyinq` (input) and
`struct ttyoutq` (output) are defined in `sys/sys/ttyqueue.h`:

```c
/* sys/sys/ttyqueue.h */
struct ttyinq {
	struct ttyinq_block	*ti_firstblock;
	struct ttyinq_block	*ti_startblock;
	struct ttyinq_block	*ti_reprintblock;
	struct ttyinq_block	*ti_lastblock;
	unsigned int		ti_begin;
	unsigned int		ti_linestart;
	unsigned int		ti_reprint;
	unsigned int		ti_end;
	unsigned int		ti_nblocks;
	unsigned int		ti_quota;
};
#define TTYINQ_DATASIZE 128

struct ttyoutq {
	struct ttyoutq_block	*to_firstblock;
	struct ttyoutq_block	*to_lastblock;
	unsigned int		to_begin;
	unsigned int		to_end;
	unsigned int		to_nblocks;
	unsigned int		to_quota;
};
#define TTYOUTQ_DATASIZE (256 - sizeof(struct ttyoutq_block *))
```

The input queue carries extra cursors the output queue does not: `ti_startblock`/
`ti_begin` mark the start of the current line, `ti_linestart` the end of the last
canonicalized line, and `ti_reprintblock`/`ti_reprint` the position of the cursor
for re-echoing a line (needed for line editing like Ctrl-U erase-to-start). The
block lists exist because a terminal line can be longer than one 128-byte block;
the queue grows by appending `ttyinq_block`s up to `ti_quota`.

`struct ttydevsw` is the terminal driver's method table, the TTY analogue of
`cdevsw`. From `sys/sys/ttydevsw.h`:

```c
/* sys/sys/ttydevsw.h */
struct ttydevsw {
	unsigned int	tsw_flags;	/* Default TTY flags. */
	tsw_open_t	*tsw_open;	/* Device opening. */
	tsw_close_t	*tsw_close;	/* Device closure. */
	tsw_outwakeup_t	*tsw_outwakeup;	/* Output available. */
	tsw_inwakeup_t	*tsw_inwakeup;	/* Input can be stored again. */
	tsw_ioctl_t	*tsw_ioctl;	/* ioctl() hooks. */
	tsw_cioctl_t	*tsw_cioctl;	/* ioctl() on control devices. */
	tsw_param_t	*tsw_param;	/* TIOCSETA device parameter setting. */
	tsw_modem_t	*tsw_modem;	/* Modem sigon/sigoff. */
	tsw_mmap_t	*tsw_mmap;	/* mmap() hooks. */
	tsw_pktnotify_t	*tsw_pktnotify;	/* TIOCPKT events. */
	tsw_free_t	*tsw_free;	/* Destructor. */
	tsw_busy_t	*tsw_busy;	/* Draining output. */
	void		*tsw_spare[3];	/* For future use. */
};
```

`struct pts_softc` (in `sys/kern/tty_pts.c`) is the per-pseudo-terminal state. It
holds the two blocking primitives that make the master side behave like a pipe:

```c
/* sys/kern/tty_pts.c */
struct pts_softc {
	int		pts_unit;	/* (c) Device unit number. */
	unsigned int	pts_flags;	/* (t) Device flags. */
#define	PTS_PKT		0x1	/* Packet mode. */
#define	PTS_FINISHED	0x2	/* Return errors on read()/write(). */
	char		pts_pkt;	/* (t) Unread packet mode data. */

	struct cv	pts_inwait;	/* (t) Blocking write() on master. */
	struct selinfo	pts_inpoll;	/* (t) Select queue for write(). */
	struct cv	pts_outwait;	/* (t) Blocking read() on master. */
	struct selinfo	pts_outpoll;	/* (t) Select queue for read(). */

#ifdef PTS_EXTERNAL
	struct cdev	*pts_cdev;	/* (c) Master device node. */
#endif /* PTS_EXTERNAL */

	struct ucred	*pts_cred;	/* (c) Resource limit. */
};
```

`pts_inwait`/`pts_outwait` are the condition variables that block a [`write(2)`](../../lib/libsys/write.2) to
the master when the slave's input queue is full and a [`read(2)`](../../lib/libsys/read.2) from the master when
the slave's output queue is empty. `pts_cdev` is the master's own `cdev`, kept so
the slave side can find its pair.
## Deep Dive

### make_dev: what it creates

`make_dev()` is a variadic macro in `sys/sys/conf.h` that formats a name and calls
`make_dev_credv()` in `sys/kern/kern_conf.c`. The work happens in three steps.
First, `devfs_alloc()` in `devfs_devs.c` mallocs a `struct cdev_priv` (tagged
`M_CDEVP`, name `"DEVFS1"`) and hands back a pointer to its embedded `cdp_c`, which
is the `struct cdev` the driver sees. Second, the caller fills in `si_devsw`,
`si_drv1`, the name, uid/gid/mode, and the `si_flags`. Third, `devfs_create()`
assigns an inode number from the `devfs_inos` unique-number pool, links the
`cdev_priv` into `cdevp_list` under `devmtx`, and schedules the devfs mount to
materialize a dirent for it.

```c
/* sys/kern/kern_conf.c, make_dev_credv() (abridged) */
static int
make_dev_credv(int flags, struct cdev **dres, struct cdevsw *devsw,
    int unit, struct ucred *cr, uid_t uid, gid_t gid, int mode, const char *fmt,
    va_list ap)
{
	...
	dev = devfs_alloc(flags);
	...
	snprintf(dev->si_name, sizeof(dev->si_name), fmt, __va_arg(ap));
	...
	dev->si_devsw = devsw;
	dev->si_uid = uid;
	dev->si_gid = gid;
	dev->si_mode = mode;
	...
	devfs_create(dev);
	...
}
```

A driver's attach routine typically does exactly this: build a static `cdevsw`,
allocate a softc, point `si_drv1` at it, and call `make_dev()`. The return is the
`struct cdev *`, which the driver stores in its softc so it can `destroy_dev()` it
on detach.

### The read path: from vnode to d_read

When userland calls [`read(2)`](../../lib/libsys/read.2) on a devfs file descriptor, the VFS layer resolves
the vnode and calls its read operation. For devfs that is `devfs_read_f()` in
`devfs_vnops.c`. The first thing it does is recover the `cdev` and `cdevsw` from
the file, via `devfs_fp_check()`:

```c
/* sys/fs/devfs/devfs_vnops.c */
static int
devfs_fp_check(struct file *fp, struct cdev **devp, struct cdevsw **dswp,
    int *ref)
{
	*dswp = devvn_refthread(fp->f_vnode, devp, ref);
	if (*dswp == NULL || *devp != fp->f_data) {
		if (*dswp != NULL)
			dev_relthread(*devp, *ref);
		return (ENXIO);
	}
	KASSERT((*devp)->si_refcount > 0,
	    ("devfs: un-referenced struct cdev *(%s)", devtoname(*devp)));
	if (*dswp == NULL)
		return (ENXIO);
	curthread->td_fpop = fp;
	return (0);
}
```

`devvn_refthread()` is the key: it takes the vnode, finds the `cdev_priv` that owns
it, and returns both the `cdev` (in `*devp`) and its `cdevsw` (in `*dswp`), while
bumping the reference count so the device cannot be torn down mid-read. Storing
`curthread->td_fpop = fp` (curthread is the kernel macro for the currently running
thread) is what lets the driver later call `devfs_get_cdevpriv()` to reach its
per-file data. `devfs_read_f()` then calls `dswp->d_read(*devp, uio, ioflag,
active_cred, td)`. Inside the driver, the copy into user space is `uiomove()`:

```c
/* sys/kern/subr_uio.c (signature) */
int
uiomove(void *buf, size_t len, struct uio *uio)
{
	...
}
```

`uiomove()` walks the `uio`'s iovec array, copies `len` bytes between the kernel
buffer `buf` and user space, and updates `uio->uio_resid` and `uio->uio_offset`.
For a `UIO_READ` it copies kernel→user, for `UIO_WRITE` user→kernel. A driver's
`d_read` therefore looks like: fill a kernel buffer from the device, then
`uiomove(kbuf, n, uio)`, returning the number of bytes moved. The same function
serves `d_write`, and `uiomove_nofault()` is the variant used where page faults must
be disabled (for example, in interrupt context).

### devfs: where the /dev entries come from

devfs is a kernel-populated filesystem. It has no on-disk data; its "contents" are
the `cdevp_list` in `devfs_devs.c`. When a process does `lookup(9)` on a path under
`/dev`, `devfs_lookup()` in `devfs_vnops.c` asks `devfs_find()` to match the name
against the list and return the owning `cdev_priv`. If the device is a *clone*
device (one `cdevsw` that backs many instances, like `/dev/pts/*` or
`/dev/uart/*`), `clone_create()` in `kern_conf.c` instantiates a new `cdev` on
demand, calls the driver's `clone_setup`/`clone_create` callbacks, and links it as a
child. This is why you can `open("/dev/pts/123")` for a pty that did not exist a
moment ago: the lookup creates it.

The per-jail view is applied at this same point. Each devfs mount has a
`dm_ruleset` (see `struct devfs_mount`). When a dirent is being materialized for a
particular mount, `devfs_ruleset_applyde()` in `devfs_rule.c` walks the rules and
lets them rewrite the node's uid/gid/mode or set it to a whiteout. The base system
mount uses a ruleset that hides nothing; a jail's mount uses a ruleset built from
its `devfs_rules` that hides, say, all of `/dev` except the console and the pty
nodes it needs. `devfs_prison_check()` in `devfs_vnops.c` is the gate that decides
whether a given mount (and thus a given jail) is allowed to see a node at all. The
net effect: one physical device list, many different `/dev` trees, selected by
which ruleset the mount carries.
### The line discipline: bytes to lines

The terminal's `d_read` is `ttydev_read()` in `sys/kern/tty.c`; it pulls bytes out
of the input queue and hands them to the line discipline. The discipline's input
entry is `ttydisc_getc()` in `sys/kern/tty_ttydisc.c`, which processes one byte at a
time according to `t_termios`. In canonical mode (`ICANON` set in `c_lflag`), the
path is:

1. **Input processing** (`c_iflag`): strip or mark parity errors, translate
   `
`→`
` (`ICRNL`), strip high bit (`ISTRIP`), and honor software flow control
   (`IXON`/`IXOFF`) — a Ctrl-S stops the output queue, a Ctrl-Q resumes it.
2. **Canonical accumulation**: the byte is appended to `t_inq` via
   `ttyinq_write()`. If `ISIG` is set, special characters are intercepted *before*
   they reach the line buffer: Ctrl-C (`VINTR`) sends `SIGINT`, Ctrl-Z (`VSUSP`)
   sends `SIGTSTP`, Ctrl-U (`VERASE`) erases. The targets are the processes
   in `t_pgrp`, the foreground process group.
3. **Echo** (`ECHO` in `c_lflag`): each printable byte is written back to the
   output queue so the user sees what they typed; control characters are echoed in
   `^X` notation by the `CTL_PRINT`/`CTL_ECHO` macros at the top of the file.
4. **Line completion**: when a newline (or `VEOL`) arrives, the line is
   "canonicalized" — `ttyinq_canonicalize()` moves `ti_linestart` past it — and the
   reader's [`read(2)`](../../lib/libsys/read.2) wakes up, returning the line.

The signal generation is the part that connects to the Signals/IPC (inter-process
communication) chapter: the discipline computes the target process group from
`t_pgrp` and queues the signal there; the actual delivery is the signal subsystem's
job. The `CMP_CC` and `CMP_FLAG` macros at the top of `tty_ttydisc.c` are the
compact way the code tests "does this byte equal the configured `VINTR`?" and "is
`ICANON` on?":

```c
/* sys/kern/tty_ttydisc.c */
#define	CMP_CC(v,c) (tp->t_termios.c_cc[v] != _POSIX_VDISABLE && 			tp->t_termios.c_cc[v] == (c))
#define	CMP_FLAG(field,opt) (tp->t_termios.c_ ## field ## flag & (opt))
```

In non-canonical mode (`ICANON` clear), step 4 never happens and `ttydisc_getc_poll`
reports a byte as soon as any is available; this is what `vi`-style editors and
`raw` mode use. The output side is symmetric: `ttydev_write()` feeds the output
queue, and the discipline applies `OPOST` output processing (`ONLCR` turns `
`
into `
`) before the bytes are handed to the driver's `tsw_outwakeup`.

### Pseudo-terminals: a terminal with no wire

A pty is two `struct tty` objects wired back to back. `sys/kern/tty_pts.c`
registers a `cdevsw` for the *master* side; opening `/dev/pts/N` (or the legacy
`/dev/ptmx`) creates the pair. The slave side is an ordinary `tty` — it runs the
standard `termios` line discipline, has a `t_pgrp`, and can be a controlling
terminal — so a shell opened on it behaves exactly as if a real serial line were
attached. The master side is what `sshd` or `xterm` holds: it is a raw pipe into
the slave's queues.

The wiring is the `pts_softc` pair. When the slave's input queue has room, the
master's blocking [`write(2)`](../../lib/libsys/write.2) (which sleeps on `pts_inwait`) is woken and the bytes
are copied into the slave's `t_inq`; the slave's line discipline then processes
them as if they came from a keyboard. When the slave produces output (echo,
program stdout), it lands in the slave's `t_outq`, which wakes the master's
blocking [`read(2)`](../../lib/libsys/read.2) (sleeping on `pts_outwait`) and copies the bytes out. Packet
mode (`PTS_PKT`, enabled with `TIOCPKT`) prepends a one-byte event header to the
master's reads so the master can tell normal data apart from window-size changes
and stop/start events — this is how `xterm` learns the terminal was resized. The
result is that `sshd`, which has only a network socket, can present a fully
functional terminal to a shell: the network bytes become master writes, and the
shell's output comes back as master reads, with the line discipline doing all the
echo and signal work in between.

## Advanced Notes

**Debugging with DTrace and [DDB](README_kdb.md#glossary) (the kernel's built-in debugger).** The
character-device path is instrumented with SDT/DTrace probes in several places: the
`dtrace:syscall` provider fires around `open`/`read`/`write`/`ioctl`, and the
`dtrace:io` provider can be used to watch `uiomove` traffic. In DDB, the
`_db_show_devsw()` and `_db_show_termios()` helpers (let the `db_show_print_syinit`
family) let you dump a `cdevsw` method table and a `termios` state from a live
kernel — useful when a device is misbehaving and you need to confirm which
`d_read` is actually installed. The [`devname(3)`](../../lib/libc/gen/devname.3)/ `sysctl kern.devname` path (the
`sysctl_devname` handler in `devfs_devs.c`) is the reverse lookup from a `dev_t`
back to a name, which is how [`stat(2)`](../../lib/libsys/stat.2) output gets turned into a human-readable
device name.

**Reference counting and the deferred-destroy race.** The single most common
cdev bug is a use-after-free during `destroy_dev()`. Because a `cdev` can be
referenced by an open file descriptor on another CPU, `destroy_dev()` does not free
the structure immediately; it marks the `cdev_priv` (the `CDP_UNREF_DTR`/
`CDP_SCHED_DTR` flags), schedules a taskqueue callback
(`destroy_dev_tq`/`destroy_dev_tq_giant`), and only frees it once `si_usecount` and
`si_threadcount` both reach zero. A driver that frees its softc in `d_close`
without checking whether another descriptor is still open will corrupt memory. The
`dev_lock()`/`dev_unlock_and_free()` split in `kern_conf.c` exists because freeing
under `devmtx` would deadlock with the system map mutex; the free is deferred until
the lock is dropped.

**uiomove and the nofault variants.** `uiomove()` may fault the user address space
while copying, so it must be called with the thread's VM map in a state that allows
faults. In interrupt or soft-interrupt context, or when a driver must not block,
`uiomove_nofault()` (and the lower-level `copyin_nofault`/`copyout_nofault` in the
same file) disable page faults for the duration of the copy and return an error
instead of sleeping. Getting this wrong — calling the faulting `uiomove` from an
interrupt — is a classic source of "sleeping in interrupt" panics.

**Line-discipline locking.** The whole `tty` is protected by `t_mtx` (the
`(t)`-annotated fields), and the global `tty_list` by `tty_list_sx` (the `(l)`
fields). The line discipline runs with `t_mtx` held, so a `d_read` on a terminal
holds that lock for the duration of byte processing. This means a slow or
misbehaving discipline can stall every other operation on that terminal, including
the driver's `tsw_outwakeup`. The `TF_HIWAT_IN`/`TF_HIWAT_OUT` flags and the
`ti_quota`/`to_quota` watermarks are the back-pressure mechanism: when the input
queue is full, the driver's `tsw_inwakeup` is not called and the hardware is told
to stop, which is the kernel-side half of hardware flow control.

**Per-jail devfs and the ruleset depth limit.** Each devfs mount carries its own
`dm_ruleset`, and rules can include other rulesets (`DRA_INCSET`), so a jail's
`/dev` is the result of recursively applying a tree of rules to the global
`cdevp_list`. The `devfs_rule_depth` sysctl (default 1) caps how deep that include
tree may go, preventing a malicious or misconfigured ruleset from recursing
forever. `devfs_prison_check()` is the choke point that a mount's ruleset uses to
decide whether a node is visible at all; a `DRB_HIDE` rule turns the dirent into a
whiteout so the path does not resolve inside that jail.

**Textbook connection.** The cdev/devfs split is the FreeBSD realization of the
classic UNIX "special file" model described in Tanenbaum and in the 4.3BSD
literature: a device is a vnode whose inode carries a major/minor (here, the
`dev_t`/`cdp_inode`) and whose I/O is dispatched to a driver via a switch table
(here, `cdevsw`). What is new in FreeBSD is that the `/dev` tree is not a real
directory on a real filesystem but a kernel-populated one (devfs), and that the
tree is per-mount, which is what makes per-jail device visibility possible without
any driver cooperation. The TTY layer is the same model applied to the most
important character device: the `ttydevsw` is the driver's switch table, and the
line discipline is the policy layer that turns a byte stream into lines and
signals, exactly as the job-control chapters of the UNIX programming books
describe.
